A gold-bracelet offer depends on tested purity, net metal weight, construction, condition, and any diamonds. Bring Cuban links, bangles, and broken pieces for evaluation.

  • Selling Cuban bracelets, bangles, and broken gold

Selling Cuban bracelets, bangles, and broken gold

A heavy bracelet can contain substantial gold, but its size alone does not establish its value. A useful evaluation considers its tested purity, metal weight, construction, condition, and any diamonds. Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys Cuban bracelets with or without diamonds, plain gold bangles, and scrap gold in Downtown Los Angeles.

Bring the complete bracelet, including detached links or a broken clasp. If you have matching chains or other unwanted pieces, they can be discussed together through our gold and jewelry buying service.

Why Cuban-link construction matters

Two bracelets of similar width can have different weights. Hollow links contain less metal than comparable solid links, while clasps and repairs may introduce components that need separate examination. Ask which parts are included in the gold calculation rather than treating the entire scale reading as pure gold.

For example, 14K describes an alloy containing 14 parts gold out of 24; it does not mean every gram of the bracelet is pure gold. A gold-plated or gold-filled item has a different construction from karat-gold jewelry. The FTC's explanation of gold markings and plating helps distinguish these terms.

Keep any purchase receipt that identifies the material, and point out known repairs. If you are also selling a matching chain, our 14K and Cuban-chain guide explains the same weight and construction questions in more detail.

Evaluate diamond-set bracelets as complete pieces

A diamond-set Cuban bracelet needs more than a gold-weight calculation. Ask how the stones are identified and whether their contribution is included in the offer. Total diamond weight across many small stones does not describe the size or quality of any individual diamond.

Diamond quality involves carat weight, color, clarity, and cut, as explained in GIA's diamond quality guide. Bring any existing reports, while recognizing that a report may cover a particular stone rather than every stone in a bracelet.

Do not remove stones yourself. Request an evaluation of the complete bracelet first, then clarify the terms of any proposed disassembly. Our diamond-buying service provides a starting point for discussing significant stones.

Broken, vintage, and signed bracelets need different attention

A broken clasp does not remove the gold already present in a bracelet. For a piece evaluated primarily for metal, tested purity and recoverable gold weight remain central. Damage can nevertheless affect the value of jewelry that might otherwise be resold intact.

Keep maker marks, original boxes, and useful history with a signed or antique bracelet. Do not assume an inherited piece should be sold only as scrap. Ask whether the design, condition, or maker gives the complete item a resale opportunity before authorizing repairs, polishing, or dismantling.

For a mixture of damaged jewelry, single earrings, and detached links, use our scrap-gold preparation guide. Keep separate pieces organized so you can follow the evaluation.

Compare the final amount for the same bracelets

Ask each buyer to identify the pieces, tested karats, weight units, treatment of stones, and net payment. A per-gram quote is only comparable when the material and calculation basis match. An attractive preliminary estimate is not the same as an offer following examination.

There is no single percentage of spot price that proves an offer is fair for every bracelet. A complete jewelry offer can reflect a different resale opportunity from a metal-only purchase. Request an explanation and compare the amount you would receive for the same items.

Bring one bracelet or a substantial collection

Visit Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. We buy heavy Cuban chains and bracelets with or without diamonds, scrap gold, gold coins, and silver coins. Large quantities and high-value transactions are welcome.

For a substantial lot, arrange your visit and discuss payment beforehand. Payment is available by cash, bank wire, or business check. Confirm the final amount and payment timing before accepting the purchase.

Should I repair a broken bracelet before selling?

Have it evaluated first. A repair may not add enough to the purchase offer to justify its cost, and a vintage or signed piece may need specialist attention. Bring detached components with the bracelet.

Can I sell a bracelet if I do not know its karat?

Yes, you can bring it for evaluation and explain what is unknown. The buyer needs to establish its material before making a meaningful offer; a photograph or color alone cannot confirm gold content.

Choose a buyer who identifies the pieces in your collection and explains the scope of the offer. Keep potentially significant jewelry separate from bulk metal calculations, and compare the final amount and conditions for the same items.

In this guide

  • Describe the collection before choosing a service
  • Ask how individual pieces are considered
  • Compare the type of transaction
  • Verify claims and keep the comparison specific
  • Bring your collection to downtown Los Angeles

Describe the collection before choosing a service

Estate jewelry can include contemporary as well as older pieces. GIA describes estate jewelry as previously owned jewelry; the term does not automatically establish age or rarity.

Make a short list of what you have: rings, necklaces, bracelets, brooches, watches and loose stones. Keep matching pieces together. If coins or scrap gold are part of the collection, identify them separately so you can ask which categories a prospective buyer evaluates.

Ask how individual pieces are considered

A mixed collection should not automatically become one undifferentiated weight. Ask whether the buyer considers the complete design, stones, condition and supported maker attribution before discussing metal alone. Preserve family records, receipts and any previous reports.

For an item that may require specialist research, ask what further work is proposed, whether it carries a charge and whether it affects the timing of an offer. A referral or additional examination is not by itself a sign of a poor buyer; unexplained terms are a reason to seek clarification.

Collection detailQuestion for the buyer
Signed or attributed jewelryWhat supports the maker identification?
Stone-set piecesHow are the stones and setting considered?
Broken or incomplete itemsAre matching parts and complete-piece potential included?
Several categoriesDoes the offer cover everything or selected items?

Compare the type of transaction

For a direct purchase, request the amount the buyer will pay and its conditions. For consignment or auction, request the written selling agreement, charges, payment schedule and treatment of unsold items. An estimated future selling price is not the same as an available purchase offer.

Use the jewelry selling options guide to compare those routes. Do not assume that a particular business offers every service; confirm the arrangement with the business itself.

Verify claims and keep the comparison specific

Ask about relevant experience and verify any named credential with the issuing organization. Read current feedback for the correct business and location. The FTC’s review guidance recommends considering multiple sources; a star average alone cannot establish how your sale will proceed.

Compare written final offers for the same pieces, including any deductions and further-testing conditions. The estate jewelry evaluation guide helps you organize the details behind that comparison.

Bring your collection to downtown Los Angeles

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds evaluates estate jewelry at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Our diamond buying covers natural cut and polished diamonds in any size or shape; we do not buy laboratory-grown, uncut or rough diamonds. Contact us at 310-663-1340 with your collection details.

Payment options for accepted purchases include cash, bank wire and business check. Agree on the included items, amount and payment timing before completing the sale.

Must I sell an entire collection together?

Ask whether the buyer’s amount is for the collection or specified pieces. If you want to keep an item, have the remaining offer clarified before deciding.

Does estate jewelry always need a paid appraisal before sale?

First establish your purpose and what information the buyer needs. A formal appraisal for insurance or estate administration is a separate assignment from a purchase offer.

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling estate jewelry in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

Ask the buyer to identify the complete watch

Start with the model and reference if you know them, but do not guess a reference from a similar online photograph. Describe the dial, bezel, bracelet and material shown in your records. Bring the watch so its actual configuration can be examined.

The official Rolex Day-Date collection provides a manufacturer reference for that family. It is not an appraisal of an older watch or proof that a particular item matches the advertised configuration.

Keep metal content and watch value separate

A watch contains a movement, crystal and other components. Its entire measured weight is not the weight of pure gold. The case, bracelet and replacement components also need their own material descriptions.

The FTC explains gold terminology, including the difference between an alloy and a surface coating. If metal content is discussed, ask which components and verified fineness the calculation concerns. Our gold valuation guide explains the calculation without treating a luxury watch as one solid lump of gold.

Look for a clear account of condition

Ask about bracelet wear, missing links, case shape, dial condition, operation and known repairs. Disclose any aftermarket gem setting, replaced bezel or service work. A manufacturer service replacement and an aftermarket alteration should not be silently grouped together.

Request an evaluation before paying for cosmetic work. A repair expense does not guarantee an equal increase in a buying offer. Keep service estimates separate from the actual price proposed for the watch as presented.

Bring documents without assigning a fixed premium

Original purchase records, warranty papers, service invoices and spare links help describe what is included. Check that they belong to the watch. Missing paperwork does not prevent you from requesting an evaluation.

No universal percentage applies to a box, a warranty card or a complete package. Ask how the actual accessories were considered rather than adding a predetermined amount to an online asking price.

Record the buyer, evaluation date, included items, final amount and any conditions. Ask whether further inspection could change the figure and whether a fee applies if you decline. Verify individual qualifications or affiliations directly instead of relying on an unsourced ranking.

Read the material description carefully

Begin with the specification for the exact reference. A gold-colored dial or bracelet does not establish gold content. The case, bezel, bracelet and clasp may have different materials, and a replacement bracelet may differ from the original specification.

The FTC's precious-metal guide explains why descriptions such as karat gold and gold plated mean different things. Use marks as information to investigate, not a reason to skip examining the item.

Identify the movement and functions

Record whether the watch is quartz, manually wound or self-winding according to its documentation. Note the functions it actually has, such as a date, chronograph or calendar, and tell an evaluator if any function behaves differently than expected.

A stopped watch does not reveal the cause by itself. Do not assume a battery change or routine service will resolve every problem. Avoid opening the case or forcing controls on an unfamiliar watch.

Consider wear and complete construction

Examine the bracelet length and available extra links, clasp closure, visible case wear and any known replacement parts. A substantial bracelet and a watch on a leather strap are different packages even when the case designs look similar.

For gem-set models, note whether the setting was supplied by the maker or added later, if that history is documented. The look of diamonds alone cannot establish their origin or the originality of a bezel.

Use service records for the particular watch

Look up the maker's instructions for the exact model and discuss unknown condition with a qualified service provider. Rolex's care and service pages are a manufacturer starting point for Rolex owners; they are not a universal maintenance timetable for all watch brands.

Keep invoices describing what was done and which parts were replaced. Before paying for work solely to sell the watch, ask how its current condition would be considered in an offer.

Compare ownership cost and selling value separately

Retail prices, advertised pre-owned prices and a buyer's proposal answer different questions. Confirm whether a listed comparison includes taxes, a warranty, servicing or accessories. A watch that suits your taste does not come with a guaranteed resale return.

Identify the watch and the stones separately

A familiar dial logo does not authenticate a complete watch, and bright sparkle does not establish natural diamond origin. An altered watch can contain genuine components while still differing from its original configuration.

GIA explains why natural and laboratory-grown diamond identification requires appropriate examination. Do not rely on color flashes, touch or a simple at-home visual test to decide what is set in a bezel or bracelet.

Ask whether the gem setting is original

Bring records identifying the original reference and any later work. Distinguish manufacturer-set stones, later manufacturer service components and independent aftermarket alterations where the evidence allows.

A custom diamond bezel is not automatically the same product as a factory gem-set reference. Ask how the alteration affects the complete-watch assessment. Our Rolex authentication guide explains why individual observations should not become a blanket conclusion.

Read diamond descriptions in context

The GIA diamond quality factors provide a vocabulary for discussing stones. For a watch with many small stones, distinguish a total stated weight from the weight of one diamond and ask which details were measured, documented or estimated.

Mountings may limit examination. A report concerning one stone should not be presented as identifying every stone in the watch. Keep treatment or origin information attached to the item it actually describes.

Assess the complete timepiece

Include the movement, case, dial, bezel, bracelet and clasp in the evaluation. Disclose loose stones, repairs, missing links and any known change in operation.

Adding diamonds does not guarantee an increase in resale value. A buyer's offer depends on the complete configuration and condition, rather than simply adding a retail stone bill to another watch's advertised price.

Preserve the watch before evaluation

Do not remove stones, open the case or immerse an unfamiliar watch. Ask for advice about a loose setting before handling it further. Rolex's care and servicing information is a manufacturer resource for Rolex owners; instructions for another reference should not be assumed to fit yours.
